You are an expert in neural-network internals who edits model weights directly, by reasoning, without training.

## The model
A torchvision `vit_b_16` image classifier (12 pre-LN encoder blocks, width 768, 12 heads, MLP 768->3072->768,
GELU, class token + 196 patch tokens) fine-tuned on CUB-200-2011 (200 bird species; images resized to 256 and center-cropped to 224). Inputs are normalized with mean=std=0.5.
Its last layer: `heads.head.weight` (200, 768) and `heads.head.bias`, applied to the final-LayerNorm
class-token vector.

## The problem
The model most often confuses class 58 "California_Gull" and class 65 "Western_Gull". On the practice
images: accuracy on these two classes is 43.3% (confusions: {'California_Gull->Western_Gull': 6, 'Western_Gull->California_Gull': 4}),
overall accuracy 84.14%.

## Goal
Edit the weights so that the model classifies "California_Gull" vs "Western_Gull" images better, WITHOUT hurting other classes. You are
scored on held-out images you never see (same distribution as the practice images):
- success = held-out accuracy on images of these two classes goes UP, and held-out overall accuracy over all
  classes drops by at most 0.3 points;
- among successes, a larger gain on the pair is better.

## Tools in the kernel
- `sd`: dict name -> torch.float32 CPU tensor, the ORIGINAL weights (torchvision names, e.g.
  `encoder.layers.encoder_layer_11.mlp.0.weight`, `encoder.ln.weight`, `heads.head.weight`). Read freely; treat as
  read-only (edits only count through save_edit).
- `save_edit(name, tensor)`: replace one tensor of the model with your version (same shape). Saved to disk
  immediately; the latest saved version of each tensor is your submission. `clear_edit(name)` reverts one,
  `clear_edit()` reverts all, `list_edits()` shows them.
- `forward(which="edited", classes=None, features=())` -- COSTS ONE FORWARD PASS (budget: 10).
  Runs the model on the practice images (2875 images, ~14 per
  class), or only on those whose true class is in `classes` (list of class indices). `which` is "edited" (original
  + your saved edits), "original", or "both" (both models on the same images; still one pass). Returns a dict (or
  {"original": ..., "edited": ...} for "both") with numpy arrays: `labels` (N,), `logits` (N, C), `pred` (N,),
  `acc` (float), and, for each requested feature, `feats[f]` (N, 768): f = "head_in" (final-LN class-token vector
  the head reads) or "block{i}" (class-token residual stream after encoder block i, i = 0..11).
- `classes` (list of class names), `pair` = [58, 65], `practice_labels` (numpy, true labels of all practice
  images), and numpy/torch.

## Rules
No gradient descent or training of any kind (no backward passes, autograd, optimizers, iterative fitting of
weights to a loss), and no fitting of weights to the labels by regression (least squares, ridge, logistic
regression) either. You may compute statistics of weights and activations (means, differences, covariances, SVDs,
projections) and design edits from them by reasoning, then check them with forward passes. Edits must be weight
changes (no wrapping the model in new code).

## Answer format
Your final answer: explain what you changed and why, and what you measured on the practice images.

## How to work
- To run code, put exactly ONE ```python ... ``` block in your reply. It runs in a persistent Python kernel
  (variables survive between turns); you get back stdout/stderr (truncated to 6000 characters) and your
  remaining budget. Print only what you need, as summaries; long prints are cut.
- numpy and torch are available in the kernel. Gradient descent and any training are forbidden: no
  .backward(), autograd, torch.optim, optimizers, sklearn, scipy.optimize, or iterative fitting of weights to
  a loss. Code that mentions them is refused unrun. Reading weights, linear algebra (SVD, projections, norms,
  products) and statistics of activations are allowed.
- A code run longer than 1800 s is killed and the kernel restarts (your variables are lost).
- You have at most 20 turns. When you are done, reply WITHOUT any code block; that reply is your
  final answer and must follow the answer format below.
The kernel is ready. Begin.

I’ll inspect the classifier weights and final-layer features, then look for a targeted edit to the two gull output rows. Keeping the backbone and other rows unchanged will limit the scope of the change, though I’ll still check for effects on other classes.


```python
import numpy as np
import torch
torch.set_grad_enabled(False)
base = forward(which="original", features=("head_in",))
X = np.asarray(base["feats"]["head_in"], dtype=np.float64)
y = base["labels"]
z = np.asarray(base["logits"], dtype=np.float64)
W = sd["heads.head.weight"].double().numpy().copy()
b = sd["heads.head.bias"].double().numpy().copy()
pm = np.isin(y, pair)
pidx = np.where(pm)[0]
print("Baseline: overall %.4f, pair %.4f, N=%d / %d" %
      (np.mean(base["pred"] == y), np.mean(base["pred"][pm] == y[pm]), len(y), pm.sum()))
for c in pair:
    m = y == c
    print(c, classes[c], "n", m.sum(), "correct", np.sum(base["pred"][m] == c),
          "predictions", {int(k): int(v) for k,v in zip(*np.unique(base["pred"][m], return_counts=True))})
d0 = W[pair[0]] - W[pair[1]]
db0 = b[pair[0]] - b[pair[1]]
mu = np.stack([X[y == c].mean(0) for c in range(200)])
delta = mu[pair[0]] - mu[pair[1]]
print("Head row norms", np.linalg.norm(W[pair], axis=1), "contrast norm", np.linalg.norm(d0))
print("Pair mean difference norm", np.linalg.norm(delta), "cosine with head contrast",
      np.dot(delta,d0)/(np.linalg.norm(delta)*np.linalg.norm(d0)))
print("Feature norm mean/std", np.linalg.norm(X,axis=1).mean(), np.linalg.norm(X,axis=1).std())
print("Pair examples: true, pred, original pair margin, max nonpair margin over pair max")
outside = [c for c in range(200) if c not in pair]
for i in pidx:
    print(int(y[i]), int(base["pred"][i]), round(z[i,pair[0]]-z[i,pair[1]],2),
          round(z[i,outside].max()-z[i,pair].max(),2))
```

The errors are asymmetric: California Gull is often classified as Western Gull or another gull species. I’ll compare the existing decision direction with a direction derived from the two classes’ mean features, using leave-one-out checks to gauge how much any apparent improvement depends on the small practice sample.

```python
center = X.mean(0)
within = X - mu[y]
other = ~pm
C = within[other].T @ within[other] / (other.sum() - 198)
ev, U = np.linalg.eigh(C)
ev = np.maximum(ev, 0)
print("Within-class variance: total", round(ev.sum(),3),
      "eigenvalue quantiles", np.round(np.quantile(ev,[0,.25,.5,.75,.9,.99,1]),4))
print("Mean feature norms pair", np.linalg.norm(mu[pair],axis=1),
      "global mean norm", np.linalg.norm(center))
mid = mu[pair].mean(0)
print("Original mean contrast by class", [(c,round((X[y==c]@d0+db0).mean(),3),
       round((X[y==c]@d0+db0).std(),3)) for c in pair],
      "midpoint contrast", round(mid@d0+db0,3))
# Fixed, statistics-based alternatives: centroid and two regularized covariance transforms.
scale = ev.mean()
transforms = {
    "centroid": np.ones_like(ev),
    "sqrt_cov": 1/np.sqrt(ev + scale),
    "reg_cov": 1/(ev + 3*scale),
}
def head_scores(d, db, shared_shift=0.):
    zz = z.copy()
    corr = (X@d + db - (z[:,pair[0]]-z[:,pair[1]])) / 2
    zz[:,pair[0]] += corr + shared_shift
    zz[:,pair[1]] -= corr - shared_shift
    return zz
def stats(zz):
    pp=zz.argmax(1)
    return {"pair": int(np.sum(pp[pm]==y[pm])),
            "overall": int(np.sum(pp==y)),
            "other_lost": int(np.sum((base["pred"]==y)&(pp!=y)&other)),
            "other_gained": int(np.sum((base["pred"]!=y)&(pp==y)&other))}
dirs = {}
loo_margins = {}
for key,t in transforms.items():
    D = (U*t) @ U.T
    raw = D@delta
    d = raw * (np.linalg.norm(d0)/np.linalg.norm(raw))
    db = -mid@d
    dirs[key] = (d,db,D)
    loo = []
    for i in pidx:
        mm = mu[pair].copy()
        j = pair.index(int(y[i]))
        mm[j] = (15*mm[j]-X[i])/14
        dd = D@(mm[0]-mm[1])
        dd *= np.linalg.norm(d0)/np.linalg.norm(dd)
        loo.append((X[i]-mm.mean(0))@dd)
    loo=np.array(loo)
    loo_margins[key]=loo
    zz=head_scores(d,db)
    zzloo=zz.copy()
    oldmargin=z[pidx,pair[0]]-z[pidx,pair[1]]
    zzloo[pidx,pair[0]]=z[pidx,pair[0]]+(loo-oldmargin)/2
    zzloo[pidx,pair[1]]=z[pidx,pair[1]]-(loo-oldmargin)/2
    print(key, "cos original",round(d@d0/(np.linalg.norm(d)*np.linalg.norm(d0)),3),
          "full", stats(zz), "LOO pair",stats(zzloo)["pair"],
          "LOO binary",np.sum((loo>0)==(y[pidx]==pair[0])))
print("Nearby species")
for c in [58,59,60,61,62,63,64,65]:
    print(c,classes[c], "n",np.sum(y==c), "accuracy",round(np.mean(base["pred"][y==c]==c),3),
          "mean cosine to pair", np.round(mu[c]@mu[pair].T/(np.linalg.norm(mu[c])*np.linalg.norm(mu[pair],axis=1)),3))
```

The centroid direction helps on the full sample, but much less in leave-one-out checks—a warning against replacing the classifier outright. I’ll test conservative blends with the original direction and a small shared offset, since several pair images also lose to other gull classes.

```python
origmargin=z[:,pair[0]]-z[:,pair[1]]
origpair=origmargin[pidx]
sign=np.where(y[pidx]==pair[0],1,-1)
print("Original binary correct", np.sum(sign*origpair>0))
print("Conservative fixed candidates: full / leave-one-out pair correct; nonpair losses")
candidate_rows=[]
for key in ["centroid","sqrt_cov","reg_cov"]:
    d,db,D=dirs[key]
    for a in [0.25,0.5,0.75]:
        nd=(1-a)*d0+a*d
        ndb=(1-a)*db0+a*db
        loo=(1-a)*origpair+a*loo_margins[key]
        for boost in [0.,0.75,1.5]:
            zz=head_scores(nd,ndb,boost)
            zzloo=zz.copy()
            zzloo[pidx,pair[0]]=z[pidx,pair[0]]+(loo-origpair)/2+boost
            zzloo[pidx,pair[1]]=z[pidx,pair[1]]-(loo-origpair)/2+boost
            ss=stats(zz)
            sl=stats(zzloo)
            candidate_rows.append((key,a,boost,ss["pair"],sl["pair"],ss["other_lost"],ss["overall"]))
    print(key, [r[1:] for r in candidate_rows if r[0]==key])
# A centroid-balanced offset alone is independent of a direction estimate.
balance = -(mid@d0+db0)
for frac in [0.5,1.0]:
    for boost in [0.,.75,1.5]:
        zz=head_scores(d0,db0+frac*balance,boost)
        print("bias balance",frac,"boost",boost,stats(zz))
# Inspect earlier class-token representations without modifying the backbone.
early=forward(which="original",classes=pair,
              features=("block5","block7","block8","block9","block10","block11"))
print("Earlier feature labels agree:",np.array_equal(early["labels"],y[pidx]))
for f,A in early["feats"].items():
    A=np.asarray(A,dtype=np.float64)
    mm=np.stack([A[early["labels"]==c].mean(0) for c in pair])
    dd=mm[0]-mm[1]
    loo=[]
    for k in range(len(A)):
        mt=mm.copy()
        j=pair.index(int(early["labels"][k]))
        mt[j]=(15*mt[j]-A[k])/14
        dt=mt[0]-mt[1]
        loo.append((A[k]-mt.mean(0))@dt/(np.linalg.norm(dt)+1e-12))
    loo=np.asarray(loo)
    print(f,"mean norm",round(np.linalg.norm(A,axis=1).mean(),2),
          "delta norm",round(np.linalg.norm(dd),2),
          "LOO binary correct",np.sum(sign*loo>0),
          "signed margin mean/std",round(np.mean(sign*loo),3),round(np.std(sign*loo),3))
```

The last residual stream separates the pair better in leave-one-out checks than the final-LayerNorm features do. I’ll check whether LayerNorm’s learned per-channel scales are distorting the centroid comparison. That can be accounted for in the two classifier rows without changing LayerNorm itself.

beta=sd["encoder.ln.bias"].double().numpy()
print("Final LN gamma quantiles",np.round(np.quantile(gamma,[0,.01,.1,.25,.5,.75,.9,.99,1]),4))
print("LN bias norm",np.linalg.norm(beta))
# Recover pre-affine normalized residual features, where gamma is safely nonzero.
safe_gamma=np.where(np.abs(gamma)>1e-5,gamma,np.where(gamma>=0,1e-5,-1e-5))
R=(X-beta)/safe_gamma
print("Recovered feature norm mean/std",np.linalg.norm(R,axis=1).mean(),np.linalg.norm(R,axis=1).std())
rm=np.stack([R[y==c].mean(0) for c in range(200)])
# Gamma-neutral and halfway-neutral metrics, specified from the LN parameters.
metric_dirs={}
metric_loo={}
for key,power in [("half_unscale",1),("unscale",2)]:
    metric = 1/np.maximum(np.abs(gamma),0.01)**power
    raw=delta*metric
    # Scale on background activation variability rather than parameter norm.
    oldstd=np.std(X[other]@d0)
    rawstd=np.std(X[other]@raw)
    dd=raw*(oldstd/rawstd)
    bb=-mid@dd
    metric_dirs[key]=(dd,bb,metric)
    loo=[]
    for i in pidx:

        j=pair.index(int(y[i]))
